chapters.title: Chapter 5: Valuation in Indian Corporate Practice

lessons.title: Case Study: Valuing One Indian Private Company Three Ways

children.text: Kaveri Spices Private Limited last appeared in Lesson 1.1, where three approaches produced three very different numbers and we left it there. Now you have the tools to do the work properly. This lesson runs one company through all three approaches end to end, reconciles them into a range, and then answers the question that actually matters: what should the founder accept for a 26% stake?

body.text: A finished valuation is not one number produced by the best method. It is a range, built from independent methods that were allowed to disagree, narrowed by judgment you can explain out loud.

children.text: Kaveri Spices is a fictional Coimbatore business selling packaged masalas across South India. Lakshmi, its founder, wants to sell 26% to a private equity fund to finance a new plant and to buy out a cousin. Here is FY26 as reported.

stats.label: Revenue
stats.context: FY26, growing at about 12% a year

stats.label: Net debt
stats.context: Term loans and working capital limits, less cash

children.text: Step One: Normalise Before Anything Else
Reported EBITDA is not the number any approach should use. Three adjustments come out of the accounts and the related-party note.

body.caption: From reported to normalised EBITDA (₹ crore)

cells: Lakshmi draws ₹3.5 crore for a role a professional would fill at ₹1.5 crore
Rent paid to a family firm, below market
The godown rent is below the market rate, so costs are understated
A fire claim settled in FY26 that will not repeat
The figure every approach will now use

body.text: Notice the second adjustment goes the wrong way for the seller. A credible normalisation schedule includes the items that reduce the number as well as the ones that raise it. A schedule containing only favourable adjustments is the fastest way to lose a buyer's trust in every other number you present.

body.title: Normalise it yourself
body.prompt: Reported EBITDA is ₹27 crore. Add back ₹2 crore of excess promoter remuneration, deduct ₹1 crore because related-party rent is below market, and remove a ₹1.5 crore one-off insurance claim. What is normalised EBITDA, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹27 crore + ₹2 crore - ₹1 crore - ₹1.5 crore = ₹26.5 crore. Every approach in this case study starts from this figure, not from ₹27 crore. Get normalisation wrong and all three approaches are wrong together, in the same direction, which is the worst possible failure because the methods appear to corroborate each other.

children.text: Listed packaged food peers of a comparable kind trade at a median of about 10 times EV/EBITDA. Kaveri is far smaller, regional, unlisted and family run, so a 25% adjustment is applied and documented.

cells: Less adjustment for size, regional presence and lack of marketability

children.text: A five year discounted cash flow uses 12% revenue growth, a 15% EBITDA margin held flat, depreciation at 3.5000000000000004% of revenue, capital expenditure at 5% of revenue and working capital at 12% of each year's revenue increase. The cost of capital is 12.5%, reflecting a small unlisted company, and terminal growth is 5%.

body.title: The full forecast, year by year

content.caption: Kaveri Spices: discounted cash flow (₹ crore)

children.text: Present value of years 1 to 5: ₹51.9 crore. Terminal value at the end of year 5 is ₹18.5 crore × 1.05 ÷ (12.5% - 5%) = ₹259.3 crore, worth ₹143.9 crore today. Together that is an enterprise value of about ₹195.8 crore, with 74% of it sitting in the terminal value.

cells: Present value of forecast years 1 to 5

body.text: Run the cross-check from Lesson 4.3 immediately. This enterprise value of about ₹195.8 crore works out to roughly 7.4 times normalised EBITDA, against a peer median of 10 times before the size adjustment and about 7.5 times after it. The two approaches are landing in the same neighbourhood, which is what gives the range its credibility.

children.text: The asset approach is not the answer here, because Kaveri is a profitable going concern whose value sits in its brand and distribution rather than in its plant. It still earns its place, as a floor.

cells: Uplift on land held at 2004 cost
Write-down of specialised grinding and packing lines to realisable value

body.text: ₹86 crore is not what Kaveri is worth. It is what a buyer would get if the business stopped trading tomorrow and the assets were sold in an orderly way. Its job in this exercise is to tell you that no offer below that number should ever be accepted, because the family would do better shutting the business and selling the assets.

body.title: Kaveri Spices: equity value under each approach

cells: High. Real peers, an observable multiple, and a documented size adjustment
High. Built on the company's own plan, and it corroborates the market approach
Floor only. The business is a going concern worth far more than its assets
Presented as a range, with a midpoint of about ₹172.3 crore

body.title: How would you present this?
body.question: The two earnings-based approaches give answers a few crore apart, and the asset approach gives a much lower figure. How should the valuer present the conclusion?
options: Average all three approaches equally, since each is a recognised method
Present a range from the two earnings-based approaches, state the asset value as a floor, and explain the weighting
Pick the highest number, because the family is selling
Pick the DCF, because it is the most sophisticated method
body.explanation: Averaging in an asset value that nobody believes applies would drag the conclusion down for no reason, and equal weighting is a way of avoiding the judgment rather than exercising it. Picking the highest or the most sophisticated single number hides the uncertainty. State the range, the weighting and the reasoning, and let the reader disagree with the reasoning rather than with the arithmetic.

children.text: From Company Value to the Price of 26%

The fund is buying a minority stake, not the company. Pro rata, 26% of the midpoint of about ₹172.3 crore is about ₹44.8 crore. A minority holder cannot set dividend policy, cannot force a sale and has no ready market, so a 15% adjustment is applied, moderated because the shareholders' agreement will give the fund a board seat, information rights and a say on major decisions.

body.title: Price the stake
body.prompt: Equity value is concluded at ₹172.3 crore. A fund is buying 26%, and a 15% minority and marketability adjustment applies. What is the indicative value of the stake, in ₹ crore? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 26% of ₹172.3 crore is ₹44.8 crore. After a 15% adjustment that is about ₹38.1 crore. Whether the discount survives the negotiation depends entirely on the rights the fund gets in the shareholders' agreement. Strong protective rights argue for a smaller discount.

children.text: Before any of this becomes a transaction, the work from Lessons 5.1 and 5.2 applies.

body.title: The offer arrives
body.scenario: The fund offers ₹30 crore for 26%, against your indicative value of about ₹38.1 crore. Its reasons: the top two customers are distributors accounting for 48% of sales, the FY25 audit carried an emphasis of matter on related-party balances, Lakshmi is 63 with no successor in the business, and the new plant will consume cash for three years. The fund also wants a tag-along right and a put option exercisable in year five.
body.prompt: How do you respond, point by point?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Separate the valuation argument from the risk argument. Nothing the fund raised changes the forecast. Every item is a risk item, which means it belongs in the discount rate, the discount, or the deal terms, and each is negotiable on its own merits.
2. Distributor concentration at 48% is real and should be conceded partially. Offer a concrete plan: a target of no distributor above 30% within 24 months, with the fund's board seat monitoring it. Ask that the discount be reduced if the target is met, rather than accepting it permanently upfront.
3. The audit emphasis of matter is fixable and largely already fixed, since the related-party rent and promoter remuneration are in the normalisation schedule we prepared ourselves. Offer the FY26 audit with the matter resolved as evidence.
4. Succession is the strongest point they have. Commit to hiring a professional chief executive within twelve months, with the fund involved in the selection. This costs salary, not equity, and it removes the single largest risk to their exit.
5. The new plant consuming cash is in the model already, as capital expenditure. Point to the forecast and show that the valuation reflects it. If they want to discount it twice, that is double counting.
6. On terms: a tag-along right is standard and I would concede it. A put option is not a valuation question, it is a liquidity guarantee, and it should be priced. If they want a put, ask for a higher price, or resist it in favour of a broader exit clause.
7. Set the walk-away. The asset floor is about ₹86 crore for the whole company, and the family does not need this money to survive. Decide the lowest acceptable number before the next meeting, in writing, and do not move it in the room.

children.text: What You Now Know How to Do

body.caption: The whole course, in one workflow

cells: Establish the purpose, the date and the stake being valued
Normalise the earnings before applying any method
Understand what drives value: growth, margins, capital efficiency
Value against peers with the right multiple and the right peer set
Bridge enterprise value to equity value
Build and interrogate a discounted cash flow, especially the terminal value
Know when assets, not earnings, carry the value
Get the right professional to sign, under the right rule
Manage the business so the number is higher when it matters

body.title: Your valuation checklist, for real work
steps: State the purpose, the valuation date and the size of the stake before starting
Normalise earnings, and include the adjustments that hurt as well as those that help
Use at least two independent approaches, and let them disagree before reconciling
Document every discount and premium with evidence, not convention
Cross-check the DCF against an implied multiple, and the multiple against implied growth
Compute the asset floor, even for a healthy going concern
Present a range with a sensitivity grid, never a single number
Map the regulatory requirements and their validity windows to the closing date
Decide the walk-away number before the negotiation, and write it down

points: Normalisation comes first: reported EBITDA of ₹27 crore became ₹26.5 crore once promoter remuneration, related-party rent and a one-off claim were adjusted.
The market approach gave about ₹173.8 crore of equity value and the income approach about ₹170.8 crore, close enough to make the range credible.
The asset approach gave ₹86 crore, which is a floor rather than a value for a profitable going concern.
Two approaches agreeing is worth more than one approach being sophisticated. Always cross-check the DCF's implied multiple against the peers.
A 26% stake is not 26% of the company's value: pro rata ₹44.8 crore became about ₹38.1 crore after a minority and marketability adjustment.
Risk arguments belong in the discount rate, the discount or the deal terms. They are not a reason to rebuild the forecast.
Know your floor and your walk-away number before you enter the room, because the room is designed to move you.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Kaveri Spices is fictional, and every assumption, multiple and discount used here is illustrative. A valuation for an actual transaction should be prepared by a qualified professional, with assumptions supported by evidence, and regulatory requirements confirmed as at the date of the transaction.
